newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Harris Bank says March Fed hike unlikely.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Harris Bank says March Fed hike unlikely.

text.p: The odds of a U.S. interest rate hike at the next Federal Reserve policy meeting stand at perhaps 10 percent, according to an economist at Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal.

Tim O'Neill, executive vice president and chief economist at the bank, said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's recent mention of a potential preemptive strike against future inflation was largely "a warning shot across the bow."
The economist's view on the March 25 meeting was largely in line with the results of a recent Reuters survey in which 24 of 35 analysts called for no rate hike in March.
A rate hike in May is seems more likely, although no move for the rest of the year would be a better guess, O'Neill said.
If the Fed were to raise the key federal funds rate in May, the move would be "a toss-up" between a 25 basis point and 50 basis point hike, he said.

The economist, who edits the bank's "Fed Watch" publication, said that in his view, central bankers focus on three key pieces of U.S. economic data when evaluating policy decisions: overall economic growth, growth in the labor market and wage measures such as the Employment Cost Index.
More data on all three sectors will be available before the May meeting, so what happens then "really depends on what the package of information is telling the Fed at that time," O'Neill said.
Asked about Friday's report on February employment, the economist said he would evaluate the release on three levels.
First, he said, he would look at the employment growth rate and the unemployment rate, both of which are expected to suggest continued labor market tightness.
Economists surveyed last Friday by Reuters estimated, on average, that payrolls grew by 230,000 last month and that the unemployment rate dipped to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.
O'Neill predicted 175,000 new jobs were added to payrolls last month.

Next, O'Neill said he would look at the measures of overtime hours and the average work week. If both measures have risen significantly, such a scenario would point toward "production-side strengthening," indicating the economy will chalk up better than the 2.0- to 2.5-percent rate of growth Fed policymakers have forecast.
Meanwhile, average hourly earnings, the monthly employment report's wage gauge, was "fairly unreliable," O'Neill said, and unlikely to capture his attention.
In the Reuters survey, analysts called for a 34.6-hour average workweek, up from 34.1 hours in January.
Finally, O'Neill said he would check out the "quit rate," a measure of how many workers have left their jobs voluntarily.

The quit rate tends to top out near 16 percent at the height of an economic recovery and trough between 8.0 and 9.0 percent at the pit of a recession, O'Neill said. In January, it rose to 12.3 percent from 11.7 percent the month before.
O'Neill spoke at some length about the so-called NAIRU, or Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment.

Whereas economists had long estimated the Fed's perception of NAIRU to be about 6.0 percent, a more likely level of NAIRU for the present economy is "above 5.0 percent and closer to 5.5 percent," he said.
Looking ahead, O'Neill projected the jobless rate would creep up to about 5.5 or 5.6 percent in coming months. That may help ease some labor-market pressures, he said.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1868 ))
